804.t: From Proto-Hellenic *méli, from Proto-Indo-European *mélit (“honey”). Cognates include Mycenaean Greek 𐀕𐀪 (me-ri), Latin mel, Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌻𐌹𐌸 (miliþ), and Old Armenian մեղր (mełr).

875.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kórwos (“boy”) (whence Mycenaean Greek 𐀒𐀺 (ko-wo)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“to grow”); see also Old Armenian սերիմ (serim, “be born”) and սերեմ (serem, “bring forth”), Ancient Greek κόρη (kórē, “girl”) and κορέννυμι…

823.t: Folk-etymological adaptation of יְרוּשָׁלַיִם (Yərūšālayim), influenced by ἱερός (hĭerós, “sacred; holy”).

879.t: Apparently from ἄριστος (ắrĭstos, “best”) + -τερος (-teros, “contrastive suffix”), though the left direction has negative connotations in many cultures and languages, including Greece.

867.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew יְרִיחוֹ (Yərīḥṓ), influenced by the Greek word ἱερός (hĭerós, “holy”).

801.t: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root as τέραμνον (téramnon, “chamber”).

839.t: Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”). Cognate with English year.

873.t: Ultimately from Proto-West Semitic *gamal-; compare Arabic جَمَل (jamal) and Hebrew גָּמָל (gāmā́l), Proto-Nakh *imkal, Old Georgian აქლემი (aklemi) and Tocharian A oṅkaläm (“elephant”).

876.t: Often assigned to Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (“to fall into thinking, remember, care for”), which is acknowledged by Beekes, but he finds it unconvincing and instead derives it from Pre-Greek based on the ending of the word.

882.t: From the Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomth₂, from the earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt-h₂ (“six-ten”); see *swéḱsdḱomth₂. Cognate with the Latin sexāgintā and the Old Armenian վաթսուն (vatʻsun).

888.t: From Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydʰtis, equivalent to πείθω (peíthō, “to persuade”) + -τις (-tis). Compare the later formation, πεῖσις (peîsĭs).

806.t: From παθ- (path-), zero-grade of the root of πάσχω (pắskhō, “to feel; to suffer”). Compare the aorist ἔπαθον (épathon).

825.t: From Proto-Hellenic *wéidos, from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos (“seeing, image”), from *weyd- (“to see”). Cognate to Sanskrit वेद॑स् (védas), Proto-Slavic *vidъ, English wit; see also εἴδομαι (eídomai, “to appear, seem, resemble”).

853.t: From ἀντι- (ăntĭ-, “against”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “hold, grasp”) + -ος (-os, nominative case ending).

865.t: From θάπτω (thắptō, “to bury”), particularly from the aorist stem ταφ- (tăph-) with its metathesis of the aspiration.

869.t: Apparently from the verb πέρθω (pérthō, “to sack; to ravage; to destroy (a city); to slay (a person)”).

814.t: From Proto-Indo-European *misdʰós (“reward; salary”). Cognates include Proto-Indo-Iranian *miždʰám (“reward”), Proto-Germanic *mizdō (“meed”), and Proto-Slavic *mьzdà (“payment, pay”).

849.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰáňňō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰh₂-n-yé-ti, thematic yé-present of *bʰeh₂- (“to shine”) with an innovative zero-grade nasal infix. The present tense system includes a *-ϳ- (*-j-) progressive aspect marker.

818.t: From Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to run, drag”), suppleted in the future and aorist tenses with *drem- (“to run”).

857.t: From *αὖρι (*aûrĭ), the old locative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews-r-, from *h₂ews- (“dawn”).

860.t: From Proto-Hellenic *deiknéumi, from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show, point out”) + -νυμι (-nūmĭ), from Proto-Indo-European *-néwti.

852.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ánemos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁mos, a nominal derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“breathe”).

837.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁gʷʰel- (“to wish”). Cognates include Proto-Slavic *želěti (“to wish, want”) (whence Old Church Slavonic желѣти (želěti)).

833.t: From Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, wither”) + -ρός (-rós). See also σκέλλω (skéllō, “to dry up, parch”).

834.t: From φρονέω (phronéō, “to think”) + -σις (-sis); the former from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).

838.t: Unknown; possibly Pre-Greek, given its unusual shape and the lack of a convincing Indo-European etymology.

877.t: Perhaps akin to πείρω (peírō, “to pierce, to run through”) or περάω (peráō, “to drive right through”), see also πέρα (péra) and πέραν (péran), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to pierce”).

858.t: βάδην (bádēn), from βαίνω (baínō), with the suffix -ίζω (-ízō).

844.t: From παρατάσσω (paratássō, “to place side by side”) + -σις (-sis).

822.t: Related to ἐρεείνω (ereeínō, “to ask”), ἔρομαι (éromai, “to ask”) (which it replaced in Attic), ἐρευνάω (ereunáō, “to search, inquire”), of uncertain origin.

878.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰrḗwər, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₁wr̥ (“well, source”) (whence Sanskrit भु॒र्वन् (bhurván, “restless movement of water”), Old Armenian աղբիւր (ałbiwr, “fountain, source”), Proto-Germanic *brunnô), from *bʰrewh₁-, which is…

847.t: From Proto-Indo-European *spewd- (“to press, hurry”). Cognate with Albanian punë, Lithuanian spáusti, Old Armenian փոյթ (pʻoytʻ).

810.t: Difficult to explain as an inherited Indo-European word and usually considered to be a Pre-Greek/substrate word. Compare also Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl (“apple”).

800.t: From δύναμαι (dúnamai, “be able”) + -στης (-stēs, masculine agentive suffix).

848.t: Disputed. The word is a widely-borrowed Mediterranean Kulturwort.

884.t: From Proto-Hellenic *éuros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wéros (“width, breadth, expanse, space”) (compare Sanskrit वरस् (váras)), from the root *h₁werH-. Related to εὐρύς (eurús).

896.t: From εὐσεβής (eusebḗs, “pious”) + -ια (-ia), synchronically analyzable as εὐσεβής (eusebḗs) + -εια (-eia). The sense “dharma” is a semantic loan from Ashokan Prakrit 𑀥𑀁𑀫 (dhaṃma).

842.t: From Egyptian bḫn (“a hard stone”), b-x:n-O39 via Lydia, which was used by the Egyptians as a touchstone of gold.

830.t: Apparently from a Proto-Indo-European *kraw-g- (“to cry”) of imitative origin, similar to κράζω (krázō) and κρώζω (krṓzō).

862.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kret-, the root of κρατερός (kraterós).

883.t: From δύω (dúō, “to cause to sink; to plunge”).
